q: You're checking your car's tyres before a long journey. What's the minimum legal tread depth for car tyres?
options: 1 mm
2 mm
1.6 mm
3 mm
explain: Cars, light vans and light trailers MUST have a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tread and around the entire circumference.

q: You're measuring the tread depth on your car's tyres. Over which part of the tyre must the legal minimum depth be met?
options: Central three-quarters of the tread, around the whole tyre
Central half of the tread, around the whole tyre
Outer edges of the tread, around the whole tyre
Central three-quarters of the tread, on one section only
explain: Car tyres MUST have a tread depth of at least 1.6 mm across the central three-quarters of the breadth of the tread and around the entire circumference.

q: You're about to check your tyre pressures at home. When should you do this to get an accurate reading?
options: Straight after a motorway journey
While the engine is running
When the tyres are warm
When the tyres are cold
explain: You should check tyre pressures before your journey, when the tyres are cold. Warm or hot tyres may give a misleading reading.

q: You use your car every day to get to work. How often should you check the tyre pressures?
options: Every week
Once a month
At every service
Only before an MOT
explain: You should check your tyre pressures weekly. Do this before your journey, when the tyres are cold.

q: Your car's tyres are under-inflated. What could this affect?
options: Your windscreen demisters
Your braking and steering
Your engine temperature
Your fuel gauge reading
explain: Your brakes and steering will be adversely affected by under-inflated or over-inflated tyres. You should keep them inflated to the vehicle manufacturer's specification.

q: You notice that your car's tyres are wearing unevenly. What's the most likely cause?
options: Using a different brand of fuel
Checking the pressures when cold
A fault in the brakes or suspension
Driving mainly on motorways
explain: Excessive or uneven tyre wear may be caused by faults in the braking or suspension systems, or wheels that are out of alignment. You should have these faults corrected as soon as possible.

q: You're driving along a dual carriageway when one of your tyres suddenly bursts. What should you do?
options: Brake hard to stop as quickly as possible
Steer sharply onto the verge at once
Switch off the engine straight away
Hold the wheel firmly and roll to a stop
explain: If a tyre bursts while you're driving, try to keep control of your vehicle. Grip the steering wheel firmly and allow the vehicle to roll to a stop at the side of the road.

q: You're stopped by the police and one of your car's tyres is found to be defective. How many penalty points could you get?
options: None
explain: Some vehicle defects can attract penalty points. Using a vehicle with defective tyres carries 3 penalty points.

q: Your car pulls to one side every time you brake. What's the most likely cause?
options: Low engine oil or coolant levels
A brake fault or wrong tyre pressures
Too much fuel in the tank
A weak or flat car battery
explain: If your vehicle pulls to one side when braking, it's most likely to be a brake fault or incorrectly inflated tyres. You should consult a garage or mechanic immediately.

q: You push down on the front of your car and it keeps bouncing up and down. What does this tell you?
options: The tyres are over-inflated
The brake fluid is low
The shock absorbers are worn
The steering lock is on
explain: If your vehicle continues to bounce after you push down on the front or rear, its shock absorbers are worn. Worn shock absorbers can seriously affect the operation of a vehicle and should be replaced.

q: You check under the bonnet and find that the brake fluid level is low. Why is this dangerous?
options: It could result in brake failure
It could flatten the battery
It could cause the engine to overheat
It could make the fuel gauge fail
explain: You should check the fluid levels in your vehicle at least weekly. Low brake fluid may result in brake failure and a crash.

q: Your car is fitted with anti-lock brakes (ABS). You have to stop in an emergency. What should you do?
options: Pump the brake pedal on and off
Use the handbrake and footbrake together
Brake gently, then release the pedal
Brake firmly and keep the pressure on
explain: In an emergency, apply the footbrake firmly and don't release the pressure until the vehicle has slowed to the desired speed. You should also follow the advice in your vehicle handbook.

q: You're driving a car with ABS and have to brake hard. What should the ABS help you to do?
options: Always stop in a shorter distance
Keep control of the steering
Brake later on wet roads
Drive closer to the car ahead
explain: ABS should ensure that you keep steering control, but you shouldn't assume that a vehicle with ABS will stop in a shorter distance.

q: Your car is covered in mud after a trip down country lanes. Which of these MUST you keep clean and clear?
options: Lights, reflectors and number plates
The bumpers and the wheel arches
The roof, bonnet and boot lid
The wheels, tyres and door sills
explain: Lights, indicators, reflectors and number plates MUST be kept clean and clear. Windscreens and windows MUST also be kept clean and free from obstructions to vision.

q: You're buying a used car that has tinted glass. On which windows is there no legal limit to how dark the tint can be?
options: The windscreen
The driver's side window
The front passenger window
The rear passenger windows
explain: You MUST NOT use a vehicle with excessively dark tinting on the windscreen or the front windows either side of the driver. There are no limits for rear windscreens or rear passenger windows.

q: You're driving along when a warning light comes on in your instrument panel. What should you do?
options: Ignore it unless the car feels different
Stop and investigate the problem
Wait until the next service to check it
Switch the engine off and on to reset it
explain: You shouldn't ignore warning lights, as they could indicate a dangerous fault developing. If one comes on while you're driving, stop and investigate the problem, as you could have a serious fault.

q: While you're driving, the battery charge warning light comes on. What could this mean?
options: The engine oil needs changing
The tyre pressures are too low
The battery may not be charging
The handbrake is partly on
explain: If the charge warning light comes on while you're driving, it may mean the battery isn't charging. You should have it checked as soon as possible to avoid losing power to the lights and other electrical systems.

q: Your engine has overheated and you've stopped in a safe place. When should you add coolant?
options: Once the engine has cooled naturally
Straight away, while the engine is hot
After pouring cold water over the engine
As soon as the steam has stopped
explain: If your engine overheats, you should wait until it has cooled naturally. Only then remove the coolant filler cap and add water or other coolant.

q: Smoke and flames are coming from under the bonnet of your car. What should you do?
options: Open the bonnet and use an extinguisher
Pour water through the front grille
Get everyone out and call the fire brigade
Keep driving to the nearest garage
explain: You should get the occupants out of the vehicle quickly and to a safe place, then call the fire brigade. Don't try to put out a fire in the engine compartment, as opening the bonnet will make the fire flare.

q: Winter is on its way. What should you make sure of before the cold weather starts?
options: The tyres are over-inflated for extra grip
The battery is well maintained
The screenwash is plain water only
The fuel tank is kept half empty
explain: Before winter, you should make sure the battery is well maintained and that there are appropriate anti-freeze agents in your radiator and windscreen bottle.

q: You notice that diesel has been spilt across the road at a roundabout. Which road users are particularly at risk?
options: Lorry drivers
Tractor drivers
Bus passengers
Motorcyclists
explain: Diesel spillage is dangerous to other road users, particularly motorcyclists, as it significantly reduces the grip between the tyres and the road surface.

q: You've stopped at a petrol station to fill up. What should you never do on the forecourt?
options: Use a mobile phone
Check your tyre pressures
Pay by card at the pump
Clean your windscreen
explain: You should never smoke, or use a mobile phone, on the forecourt of a petrol station. These are major fire risks and could cause an explosion.

q: Your car's exhaust is giving out a lot of smoke. What does the law say about exhaust emissions?
options: They only apply to diesel cars
They MUST NOT exceed prescribed levels
They're only checked when a car is new
They don't matter if the car is taxed
explain: Exhaust emissions MUST NOT exceed prescribed levels. The MOT test checks that your vehicle meets road safety and environmental standards.

q: You're driving with your 10-year-old nephew in the back seat. Who's legally responsible for making sure he's correctly restrained?
options: His parents
You, the driver
The front-seat passenger
Your nephew himself
explain: The driver MUST make sure that all children under 14 years of age wear seat belts or sit in an approved child restraint where required.

q: You're giving a lift to a 15-year-old who refuses to wear a seat belt. Who's legally responsible for them wearing it?
options: You, the driver
The passenger's parents
The car's owner
The passenger
explain: Passengers aged 14 and over are responsible for wearing their own seat belt. The driver is responsible for passengers under 14.

q: You're about to make a manoeuvre in your car. In which situation don't you need to wear a seat belt?
options: When driving below 20 mph
When your car has airbags
When you're reversing
When on a short local journey
explain: You must wear a seat belt if one is fitted, but there are a few exceptions. One is when you're a driver who is reversing, or supervising a learner driver who is reversing.

q: Your passenger is pregnant. What does the law say about her wearing a seat belt?
options: She must, unless her doctor says otherwise
She doesn't need one after six months
She only needs to wear one on motorways
She can choose whether or not to wear one
explain: You must wear a seat belt if you're pregnant, unless your doctor says you don't have to for medical reasons.

q: You own a classic car that was originally made without seat belts. Which passengers aren't you allowed to carry in it?
options: Children under 14 years old
Passengers over 70 years old
Children under 3 years old
Adults in the back seats
explain: If your vehicle was originally made without seat belts, you're not allowed to carry children under 3 years old in it. Children over 3 are only allowed to sit in the back seats.

q: You're driving your young daughter to school. Until when must she normally use a child car seat, whichever comes first?
options: Until 10 years old or 125 cm tall
Until 14 years old or 150 cm tall
Until 8 years old or 120 cm tall
Until 12 years old or 135 cm tall
explain: Children must normally use a child car seat until they're 12 years old or 135 centimetres tall, whichever comes first.

q: You want to fit a rear-facing baby seat in the front passenger seat. What MUST you do first?
options: Deactivate the front airbag
Move the seat fully forward
Put a booster cushion under it
Recline the passenger seat
explain: A rear-facing baby seat MUST NOT be fitted into a seat protected by an active frontal airbag, as in a crash it can cause serious injury or death to the child.

q: You're using a height-based child car seat for your baby. When can your child start using a forward-facing seat?
options: When they're over 6 months old
When they're over 15 months old
When they're over 9 months old
When they're over 3 years old
explain: Height-based seats must be rear facing until your child is over 15 months old. After that, your child can use a forward-facing child car seat.

q: You take a licensed taxi with your 5-year-old son, but the driver doesn't have a child car seat. How should your son travel?
options: On your lap in the back seat
In the front seat with an adult belt
In a rear seat with an adult belt
In a rear seat without a belt
explain: If a taxi driver doesn't provide the correct child car seat, children can travel without one, but only on a rear seat. A child aged 3 or older must wear an adult seat belt.

q: You have to make an unexpected but necessary short journey with a friend's 6-year-old, and you don't have the right child seat. What does the law allow?
options: The child can travel in the front without a belt
The child can use an adult seat belt
The child can share a belt with an adult
The child can sit on an adult's lap
explain: If the correct child car seat isn't available, a child aged 3 or older can use an adult seat belt if the journey is unexpected, necessary and over a short distance.

q: You're carrying young children in the back of your car. What should you do to help keep them safe?
options: Let them get out on the traffic side
Let them sit behind the rear seats
Open the rear windows fully
Use the child safety door locks
explain: You should use the child safety door locks, where fitted, when children are in the vehicle. Children should get in through the door nearest the kerb and shouldn't sit behind the rear seats of an estate or hatchback unless a special child seat is fitted.

q: You're adjusting your driving position before setting off. Why should the head restraint be properly adjusted?
options: To help you see into the blind spots
To keep you alert on long journeys
To help prevent neck and spine injuries
To make it easier to reach the pedals
explain: Head restraints should be properly adjusted to reduce the risk of neck and spine injuries in the event of a collision. You should adjust them, along with your seat, seat belt and mirrors, before you drive.

q: You're driving home in the evening. Between which times MUST your sidelights and rear registration plate lights be lit?
options: Between 7 pm and 7 am
Between sunset and sunrise
Between midnight and 6 am
Only on roads without street lights
explain: You MUST make sure all sidelights and rear registration plate lights are lit between sunset and sunrise.

q: You're planning an evening journey in winter. The Highway Code defines night (the hours of darkness) as which period?
options: From sunset until sunrise
Half an hour after sunset to half an hour before sunrise
One hour after sunset to one hour before sunrise
Two hours after sunset to two hours before sunrise
explain: Night (the hours of darkness) is defined as the period between half an hour after sunset and half an hour before sunrise.

q: You're driving at night on a country road that has no street lighting. Which lights MUST you use?
options: Sidelights only
Hazard warning lights
Front fog lights
Headlights
explain: You MUST use headlights at night, except on a road that has lit street lighting.

q: You're driving in fog. Visibility is seriously reduced when you generally can't see for more than what distance?
options: 10 metres
50 metres
100 metres
200 metres
explain: You MUST use headlights when visibility is seriously reduced, generally when you can't see for more than 100 metres (328 feet).

q: You've been using your rear fog lights in thick fog, but the fog has now cleared. What MUST you do?
options: Switch them off
Keep them on until the end of your journey
Change to front fog lights only
Keep them on in case the fog returns
explain: You MUST switch off fog lights when visibility improves. They dazzle other road users and can obscure your brake lights.

q: It's a dull, overcast day. Which lights should you use to make sure other road users can see you?
options: Main beam headlights
Rear fog lights
Dipped headlights
Hazard warning lights
explain: You should use dipped headlights, or dim-dip if fitted, in dull daytime weather and at night in built-up areas, to make sure you can be seen.

q: You've had new headlight bulbs fitted to your car. Why MUST the headlights be properly adjusted?
options: To stop the bulbs overheating
To prevent dazzling other road users
To reduce your fuel consumption
To make your indicators brighter
explain: Lights MUST be properly adjusted to prevent dazzling other road users. Extra attention needs to be paid to this if the vehicle is heavily loaded.

q: You're in a stationary queue of traffic at night and the drivers behind have stopped. How can you reduce glare for them?
options: Switch off all your lights
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Use the parking brake, not the footbrake
Keep your foot firmly on the footbrake
explain: In stationary queues, you should apply the parking brake and, once the traffic behind has stopped, take your foot off the footbrake to turn off the brake lights. This minimises glare for road users behind.

q: You've stopped your car on the road for a short time. When may you use your hazard warning lights?
options: To warn you're temporarily obstructing traffic
To let you park on double yellow lines
To let you stop on zig-zag lines
To show you're waiting for a parking space
explain: Hazard warning lights may be used when your vehicle is stationary, to warn that it's temporarily obstructing traffic. Never use them as an excuse for dangerous or illegal parking.

q: You're driving on a motorway when the traffic ahead suddenly slows right down. Why might you briefly switch on your hazard warning lights?
options: To show you're about to change lanes
To ask the driver ahead to move over
To show you're leaving at the next exit
To warn drivers behind of the hazard ahead
explain: You MUST NOT use hazard warning lights while driving, unless you're on a motorway or unrestricted dual carriageway and need to warn drivers behind of a hazard or obstruction ahead. Only use them for long enough for your warning to be seen.

q: You're driving through a built-up area late at night. Between which times MUST you not use your horn, unless another road user poses a danger?
options: 11.00 pm and 6.30 am
Midnight and 6.00 am
11.30 pm and 7.00 am
10.30 pm and 7.30 am
explain: You MUST NOT use your horn when driving in a built-up area between 11.30 pm and 7.00 am, except when another road user poses a danger.

q: You're waiting in a queue of stationary traffic. When may you sound your horn?
options: When another road user poses a danger
To tell the driver ahead the lights have changed
To greet a friend on the pavement
When the traffic is moving too slowly
explain: You MUST NOT use your horn while stationary on the road, except when another road user poses a danger. Never sound your horn aggressively.

q: You arrive home late at night and want to park on the road. The only space would mean facing against the traffic flow. When may you park there?
options: Only if you leave your sidelights on
Only if it's a recognised parking space
Only if the speed limit is 30 mph
Only if your hazard lights are on
explain: You MUST NOT park on a road at night facing against the direction of the traffic flow unless you're in a recognised parking space.

q: You're parking at night in a lay-by on a road with a 50 mph speed limit. What MUST you do?
options: Leave your dipped headlights on
Switch on your hazard warning lights
Switch on your rear fog lights
Display parking lights
explain: All vehicles MUST display parking lights when parked on a road, or a lay-by on a road, with a speed limit greater than 30 mph.

q: You're leaving your car overnight, without lights, on a road with a 30 mph speed limit. Where must it be parked?
options: At least 5 metres from any junction
Facing against the traffic flow
Directly under a street light
At least 10 metres from any junction
explain: Cars may be parked without lights on a road with a speed limit of 30 mph or less if they're at least 10 metres from any junction, close to the kerb and facing in the direction of the traffic flow, or in a recognised parking place or lay-by.

q: You have no choice but to park on the road in fog. What should you do?
options: Switch on your rear fog lights
Leave your sidelights on
Leave your headlights on main beam
Switch all lights off to save the battery
explain: It's especially dangerous to park on the road in fog. If it's unavoidable, you should leave your parking lights or sidelights on.

q: You're popping into a shop for just a couple of minutes. What should you do before leaving your car?
options: Leave the engine running to keep it warm
Leave a window open for ventilation
Remove the key and lock the car
Leave the key in so you're quicker
explain: When you leave your vehicle, you should remove the ignition key, engage the steering lock and lock the car, even if you only leave it for a few minutes.

q: You've just received the registration certificate for your car. Where should you keep it?
options: In the glove box, out of sight
Somewhere safe, away from the car
Under the driver's seat
In the boot, with the car locked
explain: You should never leave vehicle documents in the car.

q: You want a cheap way to deter professional thieves from stealing your car. What does the Highway Code suggest?
options: Etch your registration on the windows
Leave the parking lights switched on
Leave the windows open a little way
Leave a coat over the rear seats
explain: You should consider having your registration number etched on all your car windows. This is a cheap and effective deterrent to professional thieves.

q: You've stopped at the side of the road to wait for a friend, who'll be several minutes. What should you do?
options: Keep the engine running to stay warm
Rev the engine now and again
Switch off the engine
Leave the engine idling with the lights on
explain: You MUST NOT leave an engine running unnecessarily while stationary on a public road. If you're likely to be stationary for more than a couple of minutes, apply the parking brake and switch off the engine to reduce emissions and noise pollution.

q: Your car is stationary on a public road with the engine running. In which situation is this acceptable?
options: When you've popped into a shop
When warming up the engine on a cold day
When it's defrosting while you're indoors
When you're stationary in traffic
explain: You MUST NOT leave a parked vehicle unattended with the engine running, or leave the engine running unnecessarily while stationary. It's permissible if the vehicle is stationary in traffic or for diagnosing faults.

q: You've bought a brand-new car. When must it have its first MOT?
options: One year after first registration
Three years after first registration
Four years after first registration
Five years after first registration
explain: Cars MUST normally pass an MOT test three years from the date of first registration, and every year after that.

q: Your car's MOT certificate has run out. When may you drive it on the road?
options: To visit friends within five miles
Only on roads with a 30 mph limit
To a pre-arranged MOT test
At any time, as long as it's insured
explain: You can't drive your vehicle on the road if the MOT has run out. The only exceptions are driving it to a pre-arranged MOT test, or to or from somewhere to be repaired.

q: Your car's MOT is due to run out soon. How early can you have the test and keep the same renewal date?
options: Up to a week (minus a day) before
Up to a month (minus a day) before
Up to two weeks (minus a day) before
Up to three months (minus a day) before
explain: You can get an MOT up to a month (minus a day) before it runs out and keep the same renewal date.

q: You're taking your car for its MOT. Which of these does the test NOT cover?
options: The horn and lights
The seat belts
The windscreen wipers
The gearbox
explain: The MOT checks that your vehicle meets road safety and environmental standards. It doesn't cover the condition of the engine, clutch or gearbox.

q: Your car fails its MOT because of a 'dangerous' problem, but your current MOT certificate hasn't run out yet. What should you do?
options: Drive it until the old certificate runs out
Get it repaired before you drive it
Drive it only on roads below 40 mph
Drive it for up to 10 working days
explain: You can only take a failed vehicle away if your current MOT is still valid and no 'dangerous' problems were listed. Otherwise you'll need to get it repaired before you can drive it.

q: You're looking for somewhere to park in an unfamiliar area. Where should you NOT park?
options: Near the brow of a hill
In a marked parking bay
In an off-street car park
Close to the kerb on a straight road
explain: You shouldn't stop or park near the brow of a hill or hump bridge. You MUST NOT leave your vehicle in a dangerous position or where it causes any unnecessary obstruction of the road.

q: You're fitting a sat nav to your windscreen with a mount so you can use it hands-free. What must you make sure of?
options: It doesn't block your view of the road ahead
It's fitted in the middle of the windscreen
It's only switched on while you're parked
It can be held while you're stopped in traffic
explain: You can use a sat nav hands-free, for example in a windscreen mount, but the device must not block your view of the road and traffic ahead. You mustn't hold it while driving, even when you're queuing in traffic.

q: You're using a driver assistance system, such as motorway assist, on a long journey. Who is responsible for the vehicle?
options: You, the driver
The vehicle manufacturer
The system's software provider
Nobody, while it's switched on
explain: As the driver, you're still responsible for the vehicle if you use a driver assistance system like motorway assist. You MUST have full control over these systems at all times.

q: Your new car has a lane departure warning system. What does the Highway Code say about using it while you drive?
options: Use it according to the manufacturer's instructions
Use it only when you start to feel tired
Use it instead of checking your mirrors
Switch it off whenever you drive at night
explain: You may use driver assistance systems while you're driving, but make sure you use any system according to the manufacturer's instructions. Don't rely on them – they're there to assist, and you shouldn't reduce your concentration.

q: Your car can be parked using a hand-held remote control app. What MUST you make sure of when using it?
options: Someone sits in the driver's seat
You use it only in multi-storey car parks
You reply to messages while it parks
You remain in control of the vehicle
explain: When you use a hand-held device to help you park, you MUST remain in control of the vehicle at all times. Don't use the device for anything else while parking, and don't put anyone in danger.

q: You want to check that your eyesight meets the legal standard for driving. In good daylight, from what distance must you be able to read a modern number plate?
options: 10 metres
15 metres
20 metres
25 metres
explain: You MUST be able to read a vehicle number plate, in good daylight, from a distance of 20 metres (or 20.5 metres where an old-style number plate is used).

q: You need glasses to read a number plate at the required distance. When must you wear them?
options: Every time you drive
Only when driving at night
Only on motorways
Only in poor weather
explain: If you need to wear glasses or contact lenses to read a number plate at the required distance, you MUST wear them at all times while driving.

q: Your optician says you have an eyesight problem affecting both eyes. It isn't short or long sight. What must you do?
options: Drive only in daylight
Tell DVLA
Nothing, if you can still read signs
Wait until your licence is renewed
explain: You must tell DVLA if you've got any problem with your eyesight that affects both of your eyes. This doesn't include being short or long sighted or colour blind.

q: It's a frosty morning and your car windows are covered in ice. What MUST you do before setting off?
options: Clear a patch in front of you
Clear just the windscreen
Clear it with the wipers as you go
Clear the ice from all windows
explain: Before you set off, you MUST be able to see, so clear all snow and ice from all your windows. You should also make sure the mirrors are clear and the windows are demisted thoroughly.
